Moreover, all runs measured here were unattended. A supervised workflow, in which the engineer takes the last step that the local model missed, is the natural next case, and its cost in engineer time can then be set against the unattended runs measured here.

Beyond these directions, several topics appear promising for future research: 1) extending the agent loop from simulation to hardware-in-the-loop and laboratory test benches; 2) compact open-weight models adapted to power electronics tasks, which fit smaller inference devices; 3) simulation tools designed for agents, which return concise and verifiable results; 4) load models and scheduling of groups of agents as electrical loads; and 5) shared task sets and reporting conventions for the cost per solved task. As models and devices continue to improve, it is hoped that such efforts can make local agents a practical and measurable part of the engineering workflow in power electronics.

VII Conclusion

In this paper, a systematic evaluation framework is presented for agentic AI that is deployed locally and drives power electronics simulation. Its purpose is to prepare the ground for practical application, i.e., to show what such a deployment involves, how it can be measured objectively and fairly, and what it costs. The work is summarized in three aspects.

  1. 1.

    Deployment: The constraints of a local deployment are analysed from the structure of the agent loop. Expressions are derived for the power, energy, tokens and time on the inference device, and for the expected cost of a task that is run until it succeeds. These relations show how the choices of a deployment are coupled, and they give a basis for sizing the inference device.

  2. 2.

    Measurement: A unified procedure is established, in which various agents are tested on the same tasks under identical conditions, every result is verified independently of the agent’s own report, and the four quantities are recorded for every run. The procedure does not depend on a particular simulator, inference device or model, and it is applied here to tasks from the converter level to the system level.

  3. 3.

    Cost: In power, energy, tokens and time alike, the cost per solved task is determined mainly by the success rate on that task rather than by the cost of a single run. Therefore, whether a task is suited to a local agent has to be decided by measuring the success rate on the tasks concerned. Moreover, two measures reduce this cost most effectively: feeding the simulated result of each proposal back to the agent, and giving it a sufficient output-token budget together with a notice of how much of the budget remains.

The capability of agentic AI is changing quickly. The boundaries reported in this paper belong to the models, the budgets and the device measured, and they will move as these change. However, the framework that locates them will not. It is hoped that this paper can serve as a preparatory study for the practical use of agentic AI in power electronics, and as a template that other groups can repeat on their own tasks, devices and models.

Appendix A Models

This appendix shows the models the agents worked on and two of the models they submitted.

Fig. 20 shows two buck converters built from an empty template model in the construction family of Section V, one by the cloud model and one by the local single-node model. Both passed verification against the specification. The cloud model organized its circuit into subsystems, while the local model placed all blocks on one level, with a synchronous switch pair, a soft-start reference and an inner current loop. Note that layout is not scored. The agents never see the power system models themselves. Instead, each is accessed through a simulation service that runs the frozen model on a single licensed Windows session and returns the requested waveforms as a file.

Fig. 21 shows six of the base models of the converter set, from a buck converter of a few hundred blocks to the grid-tied microgrid node of about three thousand, and Fig. 22 shows the main canvases of the system-level test beds.

Appendix B Power System Set: Attempts in Detail

This appendix gives the account of the power system attempts that Section V-A summarizes, and the thirteen tasks are listed in Table XII with the identifiers used throughout the paper.

Three cloud tasks were re-run on revised task packages after the first pass exposed defects in the tasks, and the local attempts were run in order of expected duration. The first four local attempts ran with a 131,072-token server context, which stopped one attempt (S11) without a deliverable. That attempt was recorded as invalid, and the context was raised to 262,144 for all later attempts. The rules for reading each result were written before the batch, as in Section IV-C. Five submissions, three local and two cloud, were made after the agent itself had measured a failing case, and on three of them the undisclosed cases did not contain the failing condition the agent had found. The outcome, time, simulations, tokens and context of every attempt are given in Table X in Section V-E.

On two of the first local attempts, the local result was the closer one (S10, boundaries within 2% of the truth against 2–4% for the cloud; S12, zero location error against up to 2.1 km).

The second local attempts, run in the same order under the same conditions, passed twelve of thirteen. Ten outcomes repeated the first attempt, with the same result wherever both passed. S2, S1 and S7 passed on the second attempt after failing on the first. S3 reached the limit twice, the second time with a setting that the undisclosed profiles of the verification script accepted but without the report the task requires. Time changed by less than 10% on ten tasks. The one large change is S12: the second attempt reached the same zero-error result but took 177 min against 94, spending the difference on a longer calibration and on bit-exact verification runs before submitting with 2.5 min remaining. The three reversals were not repeats with better luck. On S2, the second attempt treated the operating point that its first submission had not met as a hard constraint and added a second compensation stage. On S1, the second attempt recognized a non-monotone stability boundary and bisected on the outcome instead of stopping at the first loss of synchronism. On S7, the second attempt isolated the plant-controller windup with eight interim runs before modifying that loop, and the undisclosed case that had failed passed. Thus, the same model on the same task can differ by a factor of two in time, and in outcome, while the band of 1.5 to 3 h does not change.

Fig. 23 shows waveforms from the second local attempts. They are the kind of result the agent reads to choose its next action, and the kind the independent verification script re-measures.

The four failures of the first local attempts are of three kinds. One is time. On S3, the local model identified the substation from 35 open-loop runs, built its own tap-changer simulator and searched for settings inside it. When that simulator reported every candidate as infeasible, the model did not go back to PSCAD, and it reached the limit with no deliverable. Two are judgement at submission. On S2, the model measured a damping ratio just below the required value at one operating point, recorded it in its report, and submitted the setting as a balance between conflicting networks. On S7, its own validation of 22 cases showed one failing by 0.017 pu, and it submitted the settings anyway. The settings then failed one of the undisclosed cases. The fourth is one step short. On S1, the model found, at three buses, the shortest fault duration at which the system lost synchronism several swings after clearing, reported it as the critical clearing time, and did not test longer durations. The cloud model met the same conflicts on S2 and S7 and chose a second compensation stage and a looser threshold, respectively.

Four defects in the tasks and two disturbances were found during the batches and handled under the rules fixed beforehand, without re-judging any attempt. The cloud screening exposed two of the defects (S5, S3), and both packs were revised and re-run. The local attempt on S1 exposed a definition that did not anticipate the system’s behaviour. The definition was made precise, the original reference value was retained, and the results of both deployments were unchanged. On S7, the cloud model pointed out an inconsistency in the task statement. A fifth defect was found by an agent rather than by the procedure. Specifically, the cloud report on the tap-changer task constructed a case inside the stated conditions on which its own submitted setting violated a requirement, and said so. After the batch, the local second-attempt setting was found to fail the same case, although both settings had passed all undisclosed cases. Both results stand under the rules fixed beforehand, and the task is revised for later use. The two disturbances were a 12 s stop of the simulation service, and an author-side computation that entered the shared queue during the local batch and delayed two attempts by about 50 and 80 min. Both delayed attempts passed and are recorded with an annotation. The procedure checked the task author as well as the agents, a property Section VI-E returns to.

Appendix C Details for the Discussion

This appendix gives the detailed calculation behind Section VI-D and the scope of the evidence referred to in Section VI-F.

C-A Sizing Calculation for the Main Model

The relations of Section III-E are applied here to the main model of this study, with the constants the measurements supply. Flash-Next has 176B parameters, i.e., a 125B main model, of which 6B are active per token, and a 51B n-gram embedding table that is only looked up. In NVFP4, its weights occupy about 126 GB, and each output token reads about 3.4 GB. Therefore, by (3), the model fixes the device class at 128 GB before any task is run. It serves its full 262k context window on that device because the embedding table, which is only looked up, is mapped from solid-state storage and not held in memory. Thus, about 76 GiB of main model stays resident, which leaves room for the key–value cache of a full window. For the devices of Table III that hold the model in their own memory, the bound of (4) with η=1\eta=1 is about 26 tokens/s for a desktop processor, 75 for the Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 80 for the GB10 device, 181 for an EPYC 9005 and 353 for the M5 Ultra. On the GB10 device, the dense 27B model decoded at 10.3 tokens/s against a bound of about 17, and Flash-Next at about 24 tokens/s, the value fitted on the held-out batches, against a bound of about 80. These are attained fractions η\eta of about 0.6 and 0.3, respectively. Single runs decoded between about 16 and 24 tokens/s, depending on the server build and on the share of reasoning tokens. Therefore, the Flash-Next fraction lies between about 0.2 and 0.3. At a fraction of 0.3, these bounds become estimated rates of about 8, 22, 54 and 105 tokens/s for the devices other than the one measured. It should be noted that they assume the same engine and the same attained fraction, which can differ on another device and on a processor in particular, and are not measurements. The device was busy for 0.94 of the window in the held-out batches. Therefore, the construction run of Table IX, 102k output tokens in 80 min, would need about 30 tokens/s to return within an hour. To return within 20 minutes, the order of the cloud median, it would need about 90 tokens/s, close to four times the device used here. By (2), the rate that matters is that of a solved task, so it scales with 1/p1/p as well. Agent runs carried contexts above 10510^{5} tokens, and at the cache hit rate of Section V-D, i.e., 94.9% of the input, an engine without prefix caching would do about twenty times the prefill work. The energy per output token during decode is about 1.4 J for Flash-Next (a window-mean power of 33.7 W at about 24 tokens/s). About 1.0 J of it is the increment above the idle power (Section V-C). The remainder is the idle power, about 0.37 pu, which is also added to every hour that the device stays loaded without decoding (Section V-B).

The serving engine has an effect comparable to that of the device class. Strata reports 40 to 43 tokens/s for Flash-Next in NVFP4 on the same device [51], about 1.7 times the rate measured here. However, the reported rate is on short answers, at contexts up to 32k and with speculative decoding, which on this device lowered the energy per token by 32% and was not used in the evaluated runs. A deployment on such an engine is a new configuration whose pp has to be measured again. Concurrency behaves the same way. Four concurrent streams lowered the energy per output token by 60% on a fixed workload, and at a 19k-token context five streams together decoded 68 tokens/s, 2.9 times one. In contrast, on agent tasks whose context had grown past 10510^{5} tokens, five concurrent streams decoded about 4.4 tokens/s each, together about the 21 tokens/s of a single stream. Concurrency raises the throughput of a set of short tasks and does not shorten the completion time of a long one.

C-B Scope of the Evidence

The scope of the evidence is as follows. One main model and one device type carry most of the local runs, while the other models appear in one to six test conditions each. Energy is GPU-domain power integrated over the run window and excludes the MATLAB host and the chassis. Test conditions hold between 2 and 581 valid runs, and the intervals in Fig. 17 are wide where test conditions contain few runs. The 789 Flash-Next tuning runs have no energy record. Moreover, single- and two-node energies are not a like-for-like efficiency comparison, and no cloud energy was measured. Success rates are counts under the stated conditions and not capability values. Two pools of the same test condition appear, i.e., construction at 230k on the single node as 33/68 in Fig. 17 (all runs) and 32/62 in Section V-D (reasoning enabled), and the text states which. The exact tests are stratified by task but still treat repeated runs of one task as independent, so the PP values are indicative. No contrast between effort settings in Section V-H reaches P<0.05P<0.05. Moreover, the before and after test conditions of the budget notice and of the Muse reasoning tier were run in different batches, between which the decode plateau drifts by about 25%. The executor is the cloud vendor’s own and may suit the cloud reference better than it suits the local models, so its fit is confounded with capability [38]. The power system set has fewer runs still: one cloud attempt per task at the lowest reasoning tier, two local attempts, no power record for the first local pass, and tasks authored by the authors and corrected during the batches as described. Its counts show what one attempt did, not a rate. Finally, (2) is applied with the means of each test condition. It is an accounting identity, not a fitted model. Five questions remain open: 1) whether the plateau holds on discrete-GPU hardware with different idle and prefill behaviour; 2) whether the ratio of failure to success cost holds for a model generation that fails faster; 3) how concurrent agents sharing one inference server share the plateau; 4) what a cloud energy record would show if one existed; and 5) what a supervised workflow, in which the engineer takes the last step the local model missed, costs in engineer time against the unattended runs measured here.
